title: Crystoria: A Large-Scale Crystal Dataset Linking Thermodynamic and Dynamical Stability for Materials AI
authors: Ke-Xin Pang, Ze-Feng Gao, Yan Gao, Zhong-Yi Lu
abstract: Large-scale crystal databases have transformed materials discovery by making millions of structures and thermodynamic properties accessible to materials informatics. Yet dynamical stability remains sparsely characterized at a comparable scale because its evaluation is substantially more computationally demanding than conventional structure and energy calculations. This mismatch creates a critical gap between the rapidly expanding crystal-structure space and the physical information available for materials research and machine learning. Here we introduce Crystoria, a large-scale crystal dataset designed to bring dynamical stability to the scale of modern materials data. We construct Crystoria by systematically curating low-energy and metastable inorganic crystals, standardizing their structural identities, and combining machine-learning-accelerated structural relaxation with phonon-based dynamical screening. The resulting dataset contains 2,649,640 crystal structures, spanning 89 elements, 219 of the 230 space groups, and primitive cells containing 1-48 atoms. Among them, 1,793,353 structures (67.68%) are classified as dynamically stable, revealing substantial variation in dynamical stability across chemical and crystallographic space. By bringing dynamical stability to the scale of millions of crystal structures, Crystoria provides a physically grounded foundation for materials artificial intelligence (AI) and enables systematic exploration of the dynamical crystal landscape.

infographic.key_insight: Crystoria links crystal structures with phonon-based dynamical stability labels at million-structure scale, complementing thermodynamic information for materials AI.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The dataset can support AI models that screen candidate materials for dynamical stability alongside energetic favorability.
method: Curate low-energy and metastable inorganic crystals and standardize structural identities.
Perform machine-learning-accelerated structural relaxation.
Apply phonon-based dynamical stability screening.
infographic.evidence_signal: Crystoria contains 2,649,640 structures spanning 89 elements, 219 of 230 space groups, and 1–48 atoms per primitive cell; 1,793,353 structures (67.68%) are classified as dynamically stable.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not report screening accuracy or validation details, so stability labels warrant verification before high-stakes use.
infographic.paper_title: Crystoria: A Large-Scale Crystal Dataset Linking Thermodynamic and Dynamical Stability for Materials AI

title: Generative discovery of chemical reaction networks
authors: Yunhong Han, Gaopeng Ren, Yan Liu, Ronghua Zhang, Huangjiang Huang, Ruiqi Zhang
abstract: Chemical kinetics determines molecular stability, reaction selectivity and the evolution of reacting mixtures, but discovering the underlying reaction networks remains challenging. Here we introduce ReactNexus, a generative framework for kinetic-guided network exploration starting solely from reactant graphs. Generative models propose transition states and predict the full reaction trajectories connecting reactants and products, while calculations using a machine-learned interatomic potential verify connectivity and evaluate electronic barriers. On an in-distribution benchmark of 10,000 generated candidates, 80.8% connect to the input reactant after density functional theory (DFT) optimization and intrinsic reaction coordinate verification. The resulting networks uncover lower-barrier cooperative pathways and competition between catalyst release and catalyst-bound branches. In the examined carbocation cascades, coverage of known product precursors saturates after limited expansion and distinct entries converge onto shared intermediates, indicating a compact accessible reaction space. Network-derived candidate structures further assist mass-spectral interpretation of a complex nucleophilic aromatic substitution reaction. Together, these results establish a generative approach to reaction-network discovery and mechanistic analysis without predefined products or reaction templates.

infographic.key_insight: ReactNexus discovers kinetically guided chemical reaction networks from reactant graphs without predefined products or reaction templates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework can help engineers investigate reaction selectivity, competing catalytic pathways, and candidate structures for interpreting complex reaction mixtures.
method: Generate candidate transition states and full reactant-to-product trajectories.
Use a machine-learned interatomic potential to verify connectivity and evaluate electronic barriers.
Expand reaction networks to identify accessible intermediates and competing pathways.
infographic.evidence_signal: In an in-distribution benchmark of 10,000 generated candidates, 80.8% connected to the input reactant after DFT optimization and intrinsic reaction coordinate verification.
infographic.watch_item: The reported in-distribution connectivity rate does not establish network completeness or reliability for unfamiliar reaction chemistries.
infographic.paper_title: Generative discovery of chemical reaction networks

title: Framework-Conditional Open Materials Generation
authors: Maya M. Martirossyan, Hillary Pan, Philipp Höllmer, Stefano Martiniani
abstract: Theoretical predictions of novel materials rely on a variety of techniques, from data-mining-based ion substitution methods to fully de novo generative models. Each approach imposes specific constraints and encounters unique challenges when extrapolating beyond the distribution of known materials to discover new ones. The foremost goal of materials generation is to produce stable, unique, and novel (S.U.N.) structures. Predicted structures that meet these criteria, however, typically result from novel chemical compositions mapped onto known structural prototypes or frameworks. We leverage this heuristic insight to present a new generative paradigm for the de novo prediction of inorganic crystalline materials constrained by their structural framework---i.e., the unit cell shapes and respective particle positions. Our method, termed OMatG-FC (Open Materials Framework-Conditional Generation), learns via a combination of discrete flow matching on the atomic species and stochastic interpolants for the volume scaling of the unit cell lattice, while fixing in-place the fractional coordinates and the unit-volume lattice vectors, dramatically reducing the dimensionality of the problem compared to unconstrained (framework-free) generation. Our method is more flexible than existing prototype-constrained methods, demonstrating capability for discovery of unseen, stable prototypes derived from known structural frameworks. We also investigate the number of unique frameworks in the MP-20 dataset, demonstrating the propensity of duplicate frameworks within the dataset and providing a framework-split version. We benchmark the performance of our model using the LeMat-GenBench suite using three ML interatomic potentials and achieve state-of-the-art S.U.N. rate below the convex hull, eschewing the need to learn atomic packings for materials discovery.

infographic.key_insight: OMatG-FC generates inorganic crystals by learning atomic species and cell volume while keeping structural frameworks fixed, avoiding the need to learn atomic packings.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Framework-conditioned generation reduces the search dimensionality for discovering stable materials while allowing unseen structural prototypes derived from known frameworks.
method: Fix fractional atomic coordinates and unit-volume lattice vectors.
Generate atomic species with discrete flow matching and cell-volume scaling with stochastic interpolants.
Identify duplicate frameworks in MP-20 and provide a framework-based dataset split.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports state-of-the-art stable, unique, and novel generation rates below the convex hull on LeMat-GenBench using three ML interatomic potentials, without giving numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Fixed frameworks constrain the accessible structural search space, and ML-potential stability estimates require higher-fidelity validation.
infographic.paper_title: Framework-Conditional Open Materials Generation

title: PAPERBENCHX: Can AI Reproduce Science Across Disciplines?
authors: Ruoyu Wu, Zengji Tu, Aolong Sun, Tianyi Ma, Junren Li, Xinbo Xu
abstract: Before AI can be trusted to discover new science, it should be able to reproduce what science already knows. Reproduction provides a rigorous checkpoint for an AI scientist: the target claim is known, yet recovering it still requires translating an incomplete scientific description into an executable experiment and producing evidence that can be independently verified. Existing research-reproduction benchmarks largely focus on AI and machine learning, where experiments share relatively homogeneous software stacks. Extending this capability across scientific disciplines introduces a different challenge: agents must operate domain-specific scientific software, make physical and numerical choices, diagnose long-running computations, and distinguish valid evidence from merely plausible outputs. We introduce PAPERBENCHX, a benchmark of 93 expert-constructed paper-reproduction tasks spanning 12 research areas across electromagnetics, photonics, chemistry, materials science, biology, and robotics. Each task provides the source paper, a public task specification, and a domain-native scientific environment involving specialized scientific software. Agents must reconstruct a key experiment, execute and diagnose it, and deliver a runnable workflow that supports the target scientific claim. To evaluate scientific validity rather than surface-level agreement, we replay every submission from scratch and score only regenerated evidence against expert-validated criteria. Across 10 frontier agent configurations, the best configuration fully reproduces only 14% tasks under the 90% threshold. Meanwhile, mean rubric scores range from 27.53% to 59.08%, indicating that substantial partial progress rarely translates into complete scientific reproduction. These results reveal a large gap between paper understanding and reliably producing reproducible scientific evidence.

infographic.key_insight: PAPERBENCHX reveals a substantial gap between AI agents’ partial progress on scientific tasks and their ability to produce fully reproducible evidence across disciplines.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reliable AI-driven materials and engineering research requires agents that can operate specialized software, make sound physical and numerical choices, and deliver verifiable workflows.
method: Construct 93 expert-designed paper-reproduction tasks across 12 research areas.
Provide source papers, public task specifications, and domain-native scientific software environments.
Replay submitted workflows from scratch and score regenerated evidence against expert-validated criteria.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 10 frontier agent configurations, the best fully reproduced only 14% of tasks at a 90% score threshold, while mean rubric scores ranged from 27.53% to 59.08%.
infographic.watch_item: Results measure reproduction of selected experiments, not original discovery; partial rubric scores should not be treated as proof of scientific validity.
infographic.paper_title: PAPERBENCHX: Can AI Reproduce Science Across Disciplines?

title: Resisting Drying Stress in Laponite Bentonite Clay Composites, Two Step Yielding and Crack Peel Selection
authors: Tapati Dutta, Agnishikha Chakrabarti, Soham Mitra, Deepshikha Das, Indranil Chakraborty
abstract: Clay films that dry on a rigid substrate crack, peel or stay intact, and which of these happens matters for coatings, barrier layers and ceramic processing. Composites of clay with polymers have been studied widely. Clay composites, whose components differ in size and charge, are much less explored. We show that mixing the nano scale clay Laponite with the micron scale clay Bentonite reduces desiccation damage on both a hydrophobic and a hydrophilic substrate, Laponite films stay essentially intact, Bentonite films fracture extensively, and on glass most intermediate compositions are less damaged than a simple average of the two would suggest. Rheology of the gelled suspensions reveals a two step yielding in every composition, and the cohesive energy derived from it depends by orders of magnitude on which step is used, a point that any rheology cracking correlation must specify. A dimensionless cohesion adhesion index, whose sign we derive from an energy balance, is consistent with compositions that peel on polypropylene and crack on glass. Replicate experiments were performed for robustness of results. The results identify composition as a simple handle on the crack resistance of clay films and open the search for the critical crack-free thickness as a function of clay composition.

infographic.key_insight: Mixing nanoscale Laponite with micron-scale Bentonite reduces drying damage, with most intermediate compositions on glass outperforming a simple average of the pure-clay films.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Clay composition offers a practical lever for improving crack resistance in coatings, barrier layers and ceramic processing.
method: Compare drying damage across clay compositions on hydrophobic polypropylene and hydrophilic glass.
Measure two-step yielding in gelled suspensions and derive cohesive energies.
Use an energy-balance-based cohesion–adhesion index to interpret peeling versus cracking.
infographic.evidence_signal: Replicate experiments showed essentially intact Laponite films, extensively fractured Bentonite films and two-step yielding in every composition.
infographic.watch_item: Rheology–cracking correlations must specify the yield step used because derived cohesive energies differ by orders of magnitude; critical crack-free thickness remains unresolved.
infographic.paper_title: Resisting Drying Stress in Laponite Bentonite Clay Composites, Two Step Yielding and Crack Peel Selection

title: AtomSteer: Test-Time Constraint Steering for Atomistic Generative Models
authors: Pengfei Cai, Katharina S. C. Jäger, Utkarsh Utkarsh, Nofit Segal, Bowen Deng, Akshay Subramanian
abstract: Diffusion and flow matching models offer scalable approaches to generating crystalline materials, molecular conformers, and protein-ligand complexes. However, satisfying crystallographic symmetry, structural geometry, and accurate stereochemistry remains challenging. Satisfying these requirements calls for corrections that preserve the geometry already captured by the pretrained model. In this work, we propose AtomSteer, a test-time inference framework for steering pretrained atomistic generative models with structural constraints. During sampling, AtomSteer corrects intermediate structure predictions with bounded local projections, graph-rigid stereochemical transformations, and projections over periodic symmetries, accepting updates that improve constraint satisfaction while limiting changes to the rest of the structure. We demonstrate AtomSteer across three pretrained backbones, FlowMM, ET-Flow, and Boltz-2, spanning de novo crystal generation and crystal structure prediction, molecular conformer generation, and protein-ligand complex structure prediction. AtomSteer improves space-group distribution coverage in de novo crystal generation and improves target space-group recovery in crystal structure prediction. AtomSteer improves molecular validity and E/Z stereochemical accuracy while retaining conformer ensemble fidelity. For protein-ligand complexes, AtomSteer reduces ligand E/Z errors relative to experimental reference structures while achieving competitive docking success and PoseBusters validity. Our method provides a unified framework for adding chemical and crystallographic control to existing atomistic generative models without retraining or architectural changes.

infographic.key_insight: AtomSteer adds structural constraint control to pretrained atomistic generative models at inference time, without retraining or architectural changes.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework helps generate crystals, molecular conformers, and protein–ligand structures that better satisfy symmetry and stereochemical requirements while limiting structural disruption.
method: Correct intermediate predictions during sampling using bounded local projections.
Apply graph-rigid stereochemical transformations and periodic-symmetry projections.
Accept updates that improve constraint satisfaction while limiting changes elsewhere in the structure.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across FlowMM, ET-Flow, and Boltz-2, the abstract reports improved crystal space-group coverage and recovery, molecular validity and E/Z accuracy, and fewer ligand E/Z errors with competitive docking success and PoseBusters validity.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify inference overhead or improvement magnitudes, leaving deployment cost and practical gains to be assessed.
infographic.paper_title: AtomSteer: Test-Time Constraint Steering for Atomistic Generative Models

title: First-Principles Identification of Higher-Order Configurational Energy Terms and Their Magnetic-State Dependence in Lithium-Rich Oxyfluorides: From QUBO to HUBO
authors: Joonho Bae
abstract: In this work, we use spin-polarized density functional theory (DFT) to identify substantial third-order, nonadditive configurational energy contributions in lithium-rich oxyfluorides that quadratic unconstrained binary optimization (QUBO) models cannot represent. We test the extension from QUBO to higher-order unconstrained binary optimization (HUBO) in two disordered-rocksalt cathode materials, Li$_2$MnO$_2$F (LMOF) and Li$_2$Mn$_{0.5}$Ti$_{0.5}$O$_2$F (LMTiOF), using composition-preserving DFT energy maps. Using fixed-geometry energy maps, we show that cubic HUBO captures nonadditive contributions absent from QUBO models and substantially reduces fitting errors in both materials. Direct DFT energy differences confirm third-order nonadditivity, while comparisons of magnetic initializations reveal a strong dependence of the LMTiOF contribution on the converged electronic state. These results support the inclusion of higher-order terms when modeling configurational energetics and highlight the need to account for magnetic-state dependence in constructing DFT energy maps. The extracted terms describe effective couplings among composition-preserving exchange variables, rather than uniquely identified microscopic three-atom interactions.

infographic.key_insight: Cubic HUBO captures substantial third-order configurational energy contributions in lithium-rich oxyfluorides that quadratic QUBO models cannot represent.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Higher-order energy models could improve configurational modeling of disordered-rocksalt cathodes, provided magnetic-state dependence is accounted for.
method: Compute composition-preserving, fixed-geometry energy maps using spin-polarized DFT for LMOF and LMTiOF.
Compare quadratic QUBO and cubic HUBO fits and verify nonadditivity through direct DFT energy differences.
Compare magnetic initializations to assess dependence on the converged electronic state.
infographic.evidence_signal: Cubic HUBO substantially reduces fitting errors in both materials, while LMTiOF shows strong dependence of its third-order contribution on the converged electronic state.
infographic.watch_item: Extracted higher-order terms are effective couplings among composition-preserving exchange variables, not uniquely identified microscopic three-atom interactions.
infographic.paper_title: First-Principles Identification of Higher-Order Configurational Energy Terms and Their Magnetic-State Dependence in Lithium-Rich Oxyfluorides: From QUBO to HUBO

title: Excitons in solid molecular hydrogen from quantum Monte Carlo
authors: Edgar Josué Landinez Borda, Ravindra Shinde, Claudia Filippi, Markus Holzmann, Saverio Moroni
abstract: We use quantum Monte Carlo (QMC) methods to investigate the lowest neutral excitation of solid molecular hydrogen in phase-I under increasing compression, with emphasis on structural and response properties. We employ QMC wave functions for the excited state that feature only a single orbital substitution, or a multideterminant expansion including every single particle-hole transition, and compare the results with the Bethe-Salpeter equation (BSE) and time-dependent density-functional theory (TDDFT). We examine a number of nuclear configurations representing thermal and quantum fluctuations. The effect of the multideterminant expansion is marginal on the QMC excitation energies but crucial on the exciton localization and related quantities, irrespective of full optimization and imaginary time projection. In the strong insulating regime at low density, multideterminant QMC results match and in some cases surpass the degree of localization afforded by BSE. A similar trend is observed for transition dipole moments and excitation-induced forces, with generally good agreement between QMC and BSE but marked discrepancies for nuclear configurations where localization differs significantly. TDDFT generally gives a more extended exciton with correspondingly weaker transition dipole moments. These differences decrease upon compression, as the system approaches a semiconducting regime where multiple particle-hole transitions are less important.

infographic.key_insight: In solid molecular hydrogen, including multiple particle–hole transitions in QMC changes exciton localization substantially while barely changing excitation energies.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Accurate modeling of optical response and excitation-induced forces requires checking exciton localization, not just excitation energies.
method: Model the lowest neutral excitation of phase-I solid hydrogen under compression using QMC.
Compare single-substitution and multideterminant excited-state wave functions.
Benchmark against BSE and TDDFT across nuclear configurations representing thermal and quantum fluctuations.
infographic.evidence_signal: At low density, multideterminant QMC matches or exceeds BSE exciton localization, while TDDFT generally predicts more extended excitons; differences diminish under compression.
infographic.watch_item: QMC–BSE agreement in transition dipoles and excitation-induced forces can deteriorate for nuclear configurations with substantially different predicted localization.
infographic.paper_title: Excitons in solid molecular hydrogen from quantum Monte Carlo

title: Development and application of a machine learning potential for diamond surfaces and their sliding interfaces with silicon nitride and silica: effect of passivation, orientation and load
authors: Enrico Pedretti, Maria Clelia Righi
abstract: Friction and wear of diamond are controlled by its surface chemistry, which determines whether covalent bonds form across the sliding interface. First-principles simulations have explored the role of surface orientation and passivation, but are limited to a few hundred atoms and tens of picoseconds. To bridge this gap, we develop a reactive machine learning interatomic potential for the C/H/N/O/Si chemical space, covering diamond, silicon nitride, silicon oxide, their surfaces, interfaces, and environmental molecules. The potential is trained on a large dataset of diverse structures and is tested on multiple physical properties, including ab initio reaction barriers on diamond surfaces, and structural/mechanical properties of amorphous Si$_3$N$_4$ and SiO$_2$. We then simulate sliding of diamond-Si$_3$N$_4$ interfaces with four surface orientations, clean and H/OH-passivated terminations, and normal loads from 0.1 to 23 GPa. We identify two different regimes: one where sliding is localized at the interface, and shear stress is proportional to the interfacial bond density, and another where shear is distributed inside the softer material, and adhesion due to full interfacial bonding dominates. These results show how passivation, surface orientation and load together determine interfacial bonding and friction, with implications for the environmental sensitivity of diamond wear. More broadly, the potential enables reactive simulations of diamond, silicon nitride and silica with near-ab initio accuracy at length and time scales beyond first-principles methods, providing a useful tool for future studies of wear at plowing asperities, chemical-mechanical polishing, and properties of amorphous ceramic films.

infographic.key_insight: Diamond–silicon nitride sliding exhibits two regimes: interface-localized shear linked to interfacial bond density, and shear within the softer material dominated by adhesion from full interfacial bonding.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Controlling diamond passivation, surface orientation and load could help manage friction and wear in ceramic contacts and polishing applications.
method: Train a reactive machine learning potential for C/H/N/O/Si structures, surfaces, interfaces and environmental molecules.
Evaluate diamond surface reaction barriers and amorphous silicon nitride and silica properties.
Simulate diamond–silicon nitride sliding across four diamond orientations, clean and H/OH-passivated surfaces, and loads of 0.1–23 GPa.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports training on a large, diverse structural dataset and testing against ab initio reaction barriers and structural/mechanical properties, but gives no numerical accuracy metrics.
infographic.watch_item: Transferability to environments and wear processes beyond the tested structures and sliding conditions requires further validation.
infographic.paper_title: Development and application of a machine learning potential for diamond surfaces and their sliding interfaces with silicon nitride and silica: effect of passivation, orientation and load

title: Magnetic crystal generation with site-resolved magnetic moments via Gaussian-mixture retargeting and finite-budget yield prediction
authors: Wen-Chuang Shang, Chenyu Shen, Mikito Tsujimoto, Tomonori Tanaka, Yoshihiro Gohda
abstract: We introduce GMMag, a workflow for generating crystal structures together with their site-resolved magnetic moments, built on a conditional variational autoencoder with a graph neural network encoder and a transformer decoder. Gaussian-mixture sampling redirects generation towards selected chemical and magnetic targets without retraining. We systematically investigate how encoder and decoder design, the representation of magnetic-moment magnitudes and relative signs, and sampling choices affect reconstruction, generation quality and diversity. Because a higher screening pass rate does not necessarily yield more qualifying candidates with distinct chemical formulas absent from the reference dataset, we model how repeated generation of the same chemical formulas limits their accumulation and test the model in two separate ten-million-draw runs. As an application, the workflow identifies Nd-containing candidates with chemical formulas absent from the reference dataset, negative formation energies and high estimated saturation magnetization.

infographic.key_insight: GMMag generates crystal structures with site-resolved magnetic moments and uses Gaussian-mixture sampling to target desired chemistry and magnetism without retraining.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The workflow could accelerate magnetic-material discovery by targeting candidate properties while estimating how many distinct, qualifying chemical formulas a finite generation budget will yield.
method: Conditional variational autoencoder with a graph neural network encoder and transformer decoder.
Gaussian-mixture sampling retargets generation toward selected chemical and magnetic objectives.
Yield modeling accounts for repeated chemical formulas that limit distinct-candidate accumulation.
infographic.evidence_signal: The study evaluates architecture, magnetic-moment representations and sampling choices, tests yield prediction in two separate ten-million-draw runs, and identifies Nd-containing candidates with previously absent formulas, negative formation energies and high estimated saturation magnetization.
infographic.watch_item: Higher screening pass rates need not produce more distinct formulas, and the reported candidate properties do not establish experimental synthesizability or magnetic performance.
infographic.paper_title: Magnetic crystal generation with site-resolved magnetic moments via Gaussian-mixture retargeting and finite-budget yield prediction

title: First-Principles Investigation of Irida-Graphane: A Wide-Band-Gap Semiconductor Derived from Irida-Graphene
authors: Djardiel S. Gomes, Isaac M. Félix, Marcelo L. Pereira Junior
abstract: Opening a band gap in metallic two-dimensional carbon allotropes is an important step toward their use in electronic and optoelectronic devices, and full hydrogenation has proven to be an effective route to achieve it. Here, we propose irida-graphane, the fully hydrogenated derivative of the irida-graphene, a monolayer composed of three-, six-, and eight-membered rings, and investigate its structural, mechanical, electronic, and optical properties using density functional theory (DFT) at the PBE and HSE06 levels combined with phonon and \textit{ab initio} molecular dynamics (AIMD) simulations. All carbon atoms adopt $sp^3$ hybridization, with the hydrogen atoms of the three- and six-membered rings bonded to opposite sides of a buckled carbon framework, and the lattice parameter contracts by 4.3% with respect to irida-graphene. The hydrogenation energy of $-0.53$ eV/H indicates that the hydrogenation of irida-graphene from molecular hydrogen is exothermic. The absence of imaginary phonon frequencies confirms the dynamical stability of irida-graphane, and AIMD simulations show that its structure remains intact at temperatures up to 2000 K. Irida-graphane is mechanically isotropic, with an in-plane stiffness of approximately 156 N/m, a Poisson's ratio of approximately 0.1, and critical strains of approximately 20%. Hydrogenation transforms the metallic parent structure into a semiconductor with an indirect band gap of 4.68 eV (PBE) and 6.0 eV (HSE06). Irida-graphane is transparent in the visible range, with reflectivity below 0.3%, and absorbs strongly in the deep ultraviolet, with absorption coefficients of the order of $10^{5} - 10^{6}$ cm$^{-1}$. These results suggest irida-graphane as a candidate wide-gap material for ultraviolet optoelectronics and transparent coatings.

infographic.key_insight: First-principles calculations predict that full hydrogenation converts metallic irida-graphene into irida-graphane, an indirect wide-band-gap semiconductor with a 6.0 eV HSE06 gap.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Predicted visible transparency and strong deep-ultraviolet absorption make irida-graphane a candidate for ultraviolet optoelectronics and transparent coatings.
method: PBE and HSE06 density functional theory for structural, electronic, and optical properties.
Phonon calculations and ab initio molecular dynamics for stability.
Mechanical-response calculations for stiffness, isotropy, and critical strain.
infographic.evidence_signal: Calculations show no imaginary phonon frequencies, structural integrity in AIMD up to 2000 K, visible reflectivity below 0.3%, and deep-UV absorption coefficients of 10^5–10^6 cm⁻¹.
infographic.watch_item: These computational predictions require experimental validation, particularly of synthesis feasibility and complete hydrogenation.
infographic.paper_title: First-Principles Investigation of Irida-Graphane: A Wide-Band-Gap Semiconductor Derived from Irida-Graphene

title: Odd Elasticity in Strain-Gradient Continua: Anisotropy Classification and Non-Hermitian Elastodynamics
authors: Payam Poorsolhjouy
abstract: Odd elasticity extends continuum mechanics to active nonconservative systems containing internal energy sources, such as robotic active metamaterials with nonreciprocal feedback. Modeling these systems as effective continua requires relaxing Maxwell-Betti reciprocity, which results in stiffness tensors lacking major symmetry. In this contribution, we extend this framework to 3D strain-gradient odd elasticity to incorporate the length scales inherent in these heterogeneous systems. By applying the full hierarchy of 3D point-group symmetries along chiral and achiral branches, we derive the exhaustive set of fourth-, fifth-, and sixth-order odd elastic stiffness tensors. Further, utilizing the dynamic principle of virtual work, we formulate the equilibrium equations, higher-order boundary conditions, and the generalized acoustic tensor for elastodynamic analysis. The results demonstrate that nonreciprocal moduli survive even under full isotropy in the sixth-order stiffness, under hemitropy in the fifth-order stiffness, and under cubic symmetry in fourth-order stiffness. In contrast, the elastodynamic analysis reveals that under isotropic and hemitropic limits, despite the underlying odd stiffness moduli, the acoustic tensor remains unconditionally Hermitian. Non-Hermitian elastodynamics is shown to require anisotropy. By numerically analyzing a transversely hemitropic odd elastic continuum, we demonstrate that this symmetry reduction results in non-Hermitian elastodynamic phenomena including exceptional points in the dispersion spectra and active energy exchange through simultaneous amplification and attenuation of the elastic wave components. These results provide the necessary theoretical foundation for future multiscale homogenization frameworks for anisotropic strain-gradient active microstructures, and for the design of nonreciprocal strain-gradient metamaterials.

infographic.key_insight: Odd elastic moduli persist at high symmetry in strain-gradient continua, but non-Hermitian elastodynamics requires anisotropy.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework supports designing active, nonreciprocal metamaterials whose anisotropy enables elastic-wave amplification and attenuation.
method: Classify fourth-, fifth-, and sixth-order odd stiffness tensors across 3D point-group symmetries.
Derive governing equations, higher-order boundary conditions, and the generalized acoustic tensor using dynamic virtual work.
Numerically analyze wave dispersion in a transversely hemitropic continuum.
infographic.evidence_signal: Numerical analysis of a transversely hemitropic continuum demonstrates exceptional points and simultaneous amplification and attenuation of elastic-wave components, while isotropic and hemitropic acoustic tensors remain Hermitian.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports theoretical and numerical results; experimental validation and microstructure-to-continuum homogenization remain future steps.
infographic.paper_title: Odd Elasticity in Strain-Gradient Continua: Anisotropy Classification and Non-Hermitian Elastodynamics

title: ML-COHP: predicting bond descriptors using latent space of a universal interatomic potentials
authors: Daniil S. Alekseev, Ilya V. Chepkasov, Alexander G. Kvashnin
abstract: The integrated crystal orbital Hamilton population (ICOHP) is the standard measure of bond strength in a DFT calculation, but every structure needs its own DFT single point and LOBSTER projection, which takes days for a cell of a hundred atoms, such as a grain boundary or a catalytic nanoparticle. We predict ICOHP from the frozen descriptors of a MACE foundation model. A symmetric pair head reads the scalar and bond-projected vector channels of the two atoms and corrects a pair baseline built from the element embeddings of the same model. We tested the model on the high-entropy diboride (Hf,Zr,Ti,Nb,Ta)B$_2$, Pt clusters on defective graphene and Pt/Pd nanoparticles with adsorbed O$_2$. The error on bonds stronger than 0.5 eV is 1.6-4.1%, about half that of the Gaussian-process model of Ferreira et al. trained on the same data. Trained only on high-temperature HEB$_2$ snapshots, the model reproduces the LOBSTER ICOHP of relaxed grain boundary cells to 0.06 eV in about a second, against 5-51 hours of LOBSTER. The vector channels halve the error compared to the scalar ones, and the baseline keeps the model usable with two training structures. With geometries from a fine-tuned MACE potential, the model gives the bonding of Pt/Pd particles over a continuous O$_2$ coverage, and DFT on these particles shows that O$_2$ costs a Pt-rich shell several times more metal--metal bonding than a Pd shell.

infographic.key_insight: ML-COHP predicts DFT-derived bond strengths from frozen MACE representations, reproducing grain-boundary ICOHP values to 0.06 eV in about a second.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Fast bond-strength estimates could accelerate analysis of grain boundaries, catalytic nanoparticles, and adsorbate-driven changes in metal bonding.
method: Extract frozen scalar and bond-projected vector descriptors from a MACE foundation model.
Use a symmetric pair head to correct an element-embedding-based bond baseline.
Combine with fine-tuned MACE geometries to examine bonding across O₂ coverages.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across high-entropy diborides, Pt/graphene, and O₂-covered Pt/Pd nanoparticles, errors for bonds stronger than 0.5 eV were 1.6–4.1%, about half those of a Gaussian-process comparator trained on the same data.
infographic.watch_item: Performance beyond the tested chemistries and structural environments remains unestablished; validate against DFT/LOBSTER before broader deployment.
infographic.paper_title: ML-COHP: predicting bond descriptors using latent space of a universal interatomic potentials

title: Predicting unstable planar fault energies in multicomponent alloys from pure elemental components
authors: C Tang, J Liu, J Yi, M R Barnett
abstract: The unstable planar fault energies (UPFEs) govern slip and twinning but are not experimentally measurable. Using EAM potentials complemented by DFT, we investigate their temperature and compositional dependence and their relationship with the shear modulus. For pure \textit{fcc} elements with low stacking fault energies (SFEs), UPFEs are substantially less temperature-sensitive than SFEs. The reported linear relationship between UPFEs and the product of shear modulus and Burgers vector ($μb_{\mathrm{p}}$) holds for close-packed elements and solid solutions, but deviates for intermetallics and non-close-packed elements. In the Co-Cr-Fe-Mn-Ni system, binary alloys show composition-dependent deviations, while the correlation strengthens with increasing chemical complexity. Furthermore, $μb_{\mathrm{p}}$ of multicomponent alloys linearly correlates with the composition-weighted elemental $μb_{\mathrm{p}}$ ($R^2=0.95$), despite a systematic negative deviation. This provides a simple, computationally inexpensive route for estimating $μb_{\mathrm{p}}$ and screening UPFEs directly from pure elemental constituents.

infographic.key_insight: Composition-weighted elemental properties offer a low-cost route to screening unstable planar fault energies in multicomponent alloys through the shear-modulus–Burgers-vector product (μbₚ).
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach could accelerate alloy screening for slip and twinning behavior while reducing reliance on expensive atomistic calculations.
method: Use embedded-atom method potentials complemented by density functional theory.
Evaluate temperature and composition effects on fault energies and their relationship with μbₚ.
Compare alloy μbₚ with composition-weighted pure-element values.
infographic.evidence_signal: Multicomponent-alloy μbₚ correlates linearly with composition-weighted elemental μbₚ (R² = 0.95), while the UPFE–μbₚ correlation strengthens with chemical complexity in Co–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ni alloys.
infographic.watch_item: Systematic negative deviations in alloy μbₚ and weaker UPFE scaling for intermetallics, non-close-packed elements, and some binary compositions limit direct transferability.
infographic.paper_title: Predicting unstable planar fault energies in multicomponent alloys from pure elemental components

title: Learning Between the Lines: Interaction Interpolation in a Multi Element Machine Learning Interatomic Potential
authors: Ademola Soyemi, Kipton Barros, Timothy C. Germann, Benjamin T. Nebgen, Brenden W. Hamilton
abstract: The continuous development of machine learning inter-atomic potentials (MLIAPs)has greatly accelerated materials research in recent years. However, the need to con- struct custom MLIAPs for each unique problem remains a bottleneck which raises the question of the transferability of MLIAPs. While foundation MLIAPs can achieve transferability due to the broad coverage of chemical space represented in their training sets, their size and computational cost limits their routine use. We address this gap by developing a lightweight general-purpose MLIAP for metal alloys spanning twelve elements (Al, Sc, Ti, V, Cu, Zn, Zr, Nb, Mo, Hf, Ta, W). Here, we utilize a step-wise active learning (AL) approach to develop a compact yet diverse dataset and model that generalizes well by interpolating from previously seen interactions. The resulting potentials transfer effectively to unseen, higher body-order alloys systems, requiring only unary and binary training data to capture ternary and quaternary systems. The model also transfers well to new elements via an alchemical extrapolation within the network, requiring only unary data for the new element and its alloys. These findings suggest that MLIAPs trained on targeted, diversity-driven datasets provide transferability at a relatively low computational cost, offering a practical path toward general-purpose, resource-efficient MLIAPs for materials modeling.

infographic.key_insight: A lightweight machine-learning interatomic potential trained on unary and binary systems transfers to unseen ternary and quaternary alloys by interpolating learned interactions.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach offers a route to reusable, resource-efficient alloy simulations without developing a custom potential for every composition.
method: Use step-wise active learning to build a compact, diverse training dataset.
Train a general-purpose potential spanning Al, Sc, Ti, V, Cu, Zn, Zr, Nb, Mo, Hf, Ta and W.
Extend to new elements through alchemical extrapolation using only unary data for each new element.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports transfer from unary and binary training data to ternary and quaternary systems, plus transfer to new elements and their alloys, but provides no numerical accuracy or runtime results.
infographic.watch_item: Validate accuracy for target compositions and operating conditions before deployment; the abstract does not establish transferability across all alloy environments.
infographic.paper_title: Learning Between the Lines: Interaction Interpolation in a Multi Element Machine Learning Interatomic Potential

title: Physical structure as an organizing principle for universal Hamiltonian learning
authors: Mingkang Liu, Zhanghao Zhouyin, Guanghui Wang, Daye Zheng, Lei Shen, Qiangqiang Gu
abstract: Density functional theory (DFT) gives the electronic structure of materials, but its cost limits large-supercell calculations and materials screening. Machine-learned Hamiltonians bypass the self-consistent cycle but are usually system-specific; universal ones could cover new compositions and disordered solids. Such models must generalize across chemistry and keep downstream properties physical, while staying inexpensive for large cells. Here we introduce UniTB, a universal E(3) equivariant Hamiltonian representation framework that integrates physical priors rooted in density-functional tight-binding theory with deep learning. UniTB's network, which corrects a prior Hamiltonian, generalizes across chemistry through a mixture of experts routed by that prior and a charge-equilibration head as in self-consistent-charge tight binding. A projection bounds band shifts from the prior, suppressing spurious states and keeping downstream properties physical. We provide the fastest SO(2) tensor-product GPU kernels for the network. The variant UniTB-Flash assembles its prior from two-center tables at $O(N)$ cost for $N$ atoms, against $O(N\log N)$ on a grid. Trained on 29,242 crystals, UniTB reaches a 0.48 meV matrix-element error on nonmagnetic test crystals spanning 68 elements. Without amorphous training data, both models agree with DFT optics and conductivity of amorphous Ge-Sb-Te. UniTB-Flash ranks candidates with no significant difference from UniTB, whose property values are more accurate; together they screen 16,195 crystals for five application domains of industrial relevance.

infographic.key_insight: UniTB combines physical Hamiltonian priors with equivariant deep learning to generalize across materials chemistry while constraining unphysical electronic states.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its fast UniTB-Flash variant enables large-scale materials screening with linear-cost prior assembly, while UniTB offers more accurate property predictions.
method: Learn E(3)-equivariant corrections to a density-functional tight-binding-inspired Hamiltonian.
Use prior-routed mixture-of-experts learning and a charge-equilibration head.
Bound band shifts through projection; accelerate computation with SO(2) GPU kernels and two-center tables.
infographic.evidence_signal: Trained on 29,242 crystals, UniTB achieves 0.48 meV matrix-element error on nonmagnetic test crystals spanning 68 elements; both variants reproduce DFT optics and conductivity for amorphous Ge-Sb-Te without amorphous training data.
infographic.watch_item: The reported accuracy covers nonmagnetic crystals, and UniTB-Flash's linear-cost prior assembly does not establish linear scaling for the full electronic-property workflow.
infographic.paper_title: Physical structure as an organizing principle for universal Hamiltonian learning

title: HorizON: A Multi-Horizon Deep Operator Network for Property Prediction of Organic Battery Stacks
authors: Subhash V. S. Ganti, Lukas Woelfel, Arla Diengdoh, Tzvetan Mihaylov, Thomas Nevolianis, Jan Meyer
abstract: Transition-metal-based batteries rely on critical elements such as lithium, cobalt, and nickel. Their extraction creates environmental and supply-chain challenges. Organic electrode materials (OEMs) reduce this reliance and provide broad molecular tunability. However, OEM-based batteries still show limited long-term cycling stability. Their design also requires the joint optimization of coupled metrics such as voltage, specific capacity, capacity retention, and energy density. These metrics depend on the full battery stack and on the interactions among its components rather than on the active material alone. In our previous work, we developed a data-fusion multi-task framework for average discharge voltage and first-cycle specific capacity. Both targets are single-valued. Here, we extend that framework to multi-horizon prediction by predicting a property at every cycle of a discharge trajectory rather than at a single cycle. Our multi-fidelity and Multi-horizon Deep Operator Network learns DFT redox potentials and cycle-dependent specific-capacity trajectories within one model. We train it on complete battery-stack representations and usage conditions, so it learns battery-stack interactions rather than cathode-only effects. This framework supports long-term property prediction, inverse design, and process optimization for organic battery systems.

infographic.key_insight: HorizON jointly learns DFT redox potentials and cycle-dependent specific-capacity trajectories to predict organic battery behavior beyond single-cycle targets.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Modeling the full battery stack and usage conditions could support long-term performance prediction, inverse design, and process optimization.
method: Extend a data-fusion, multi-task framework to multi-horizon prediction.
Use a multi-fidelity Deep Operator Network to learn redox potentials and capacity trajectories jointly.
Train on complete battery-stack representations and usage conditions to capture component interactions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes training on DFT redox potentials and cycle-dependent capacity trajectories but reports no dataset sizes, accuracy metrics, or validation results.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization to unseen stack chemistries and cycling conditions remains unestablished by the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: HorizON: A Multi-Horizon Deep Operator Network for Property Prediction of Organic Battery Stacks

title: Magnetism in a homometallic square-planar Cu$({\mathrm{II})}$$_4$Cu$({\mathrm{II})}$ metallacrown
authors: Luca Bischof, Ariyan Tavakoli, Sascha Pietruska, Lena Spillecke, Ina Heckelmann, Changhyun Koo
abstract: The well-established homometallic metallacrown Cu(II)[12-MC$_\text{Cu(II)N(Shi)}$-4]$^{2-}$, comprising four square-planarly arranged Cu(II) ions surrounding a slightly off-plane central Cu(II) ion, provides an excellent platform for investigating magnetism in exchange-coupled Cu(II) clusters both by experimental and ab initio numerical methods. In the present work, sterically bulky substituents are introduced into the salicylhydroxamate ligand to obtain a modified derivative, Cu$({\mathrm{II})}$[12-MC$_\text{Cu$({\mathrm{II})}$N(L)}$-4]$^{2-}$ (Cu$_4$Cu), thereby effectively suppressing intermolecular magnetic interactions and enabling a detailed investigation of its intrinsic ground-state spin structure and exchange interactions. Static magnetization reveals competing antiferromagnetic exchange interactions of $J_1=-8.1(2)$ THz ($-33.5(8)$ meV) between the central and the peripheral sites and $J_2=-4.40(12)$ THz ($-18.2(5)$ meV) between neighboring sites on the ring of the metallacrown, which are corroborated by ab initio broken symmetry-based density functional theory (DFT). These couplings yield an $S=1/2$ ground state for Cu$_4$Cu at low temperatures, for which X-band and high-frequency/high-field electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR) precisely determine the $g$-factors $g_x = 2.028$, $g_y = 2.056$, and $g_z = 2.222$ close to axial anisotropy and in agreement with our DFT results. The ground-state spin-configuration is characterized by $d_{xy}$-character of the unoccupied states. Furthermore, our magnetization data evidence thermal transitions across a doublet-to-quartet gap of $Δ_{1/2\rightarrow3/2} = 4.8(4)$ THz which is also indicated by the emergence of an excited-state EPR signal.

infographic.key_insight: Bulky ligand substituents suppress intermolecular magnetic interactions in a five-Cu(II) metallacrown, revealing competing antiferromagnetic couplings and an intrinsic S = 1/2 ground state.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Steric ligand design offers a route to magnetically isolate molecular spin clusters for studying exchange interactions and anisotropy.
method: Modify salicylhydroxamate ligands with bulky substituents.
Probe magnetism using static magnetization and X-band/high-field EPR.
Compare exchange couplings and g-factors with broken-symmetry DFT.
infographic.evidence_signal: Magnetization yields J₁ = −8.1(2) THz and J₂ = −4.40(12) THz, corroborated by DFT, while EPR resolves g = (2.028, 2.056, 2.222) and supports a thermally accessible quartet excitation.
infographic.watch_item: The S = 1/2 ground-state description applies at low temperatures; thermal population across the 4.8(4) THz doublet–quartet gap must be considered.
infographic.paper_title: Magnetism in a homometallic square-planar Cu$({\mathrm{II})}$$_4$Cu$({\mathrm{II})}$ metallacrown

title: Autonomous Quantum Measurement with Agentic AI
authors: Eunbi Rha, Abhijatmedhi Chotrattanapituk, Mouyang Cheng, Chung-tao Chou, Shenyong Ye, Ashley S. Dale
abstract: Quantum materials exhibit diverse electronic and functional phenomena, but their characterization requires extensive experimental expertise, iterative decision-making and accumulated laboratory knowledge that is difficult to document and transfer. Here we introduce Quantum Agent (QUANTA), an agentic artificial intelligence (AI) framework for autonomous quantum-materials characterization. Using a widely adopted Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS) as an experimental platform, QUANTA combines retrieval augmentation using scientific literature, experimental protocols and prior measurements with specialized agents for experimental planning, troubleshooting, and data interpretation. A separate deterministic control layer validates instrument actions. Guided by incoming data, QUANTA evaluates measurement quality, revises experimental plans and selects subsequent measurements. We demonstrate these capabilities through transport measurements of the topological Weyl semimetal TaP, as well as investigations of nonlinear responses in magnetic material Co2MnGa. These results establish QUANTA as a generalizable framework for evidence-driven, safeguarded and closed-loop quantum-materials characterization.

infographic.key_insight: QUANTA combines specialized AI agents with validated instrument control to autonomously plan, evaluate and adapt quantum-materials measurements.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework offers a path toward automating expertise-intensive materials characterization while retaining deterministic checks on instrument actions.
method: Retrieve scientific literature, experimental protocols and prior measurements to inform decisions.
Coordinate specialized agents for experimental planning, troubleshooting and data interpretation.
Validate instrument actions through a deterministic control layer and revise measurements using incoming data.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports demonstrations on a Physical Property Measurement System involving transport measurements of TaP and nonlinear responses in Co2MnGa, but provides no quantitative performance benchmarks.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization beyond the demonstrated materials and instrument platform requires further validation of measurement reliability and control safeguards.
infographic.paper_title: Autonomous Quantum Measurement with Agentic AI

title: Comprehensive QM/ML Study of Dislocation Loop Line Segments in α-Zr Part I: <a> Loop Core Geometries, Solute Binding, and Transition Barriers
authors: Junting Zhang, Andrew P. Horsfield, Mark R. Wenman
abstract: Zr cladding alloys in nuclear reactors are exposed to high neutron fluxes, making irradiation-induced defects and solute segregation central to understanding their in-service behaviour. Dislocation cores involve short-range chemistry and long-range elastic fields, which are difficult to describe simultaneously using conventional atomistic methods. Using a hybrid quantum mechanics/machine learning (QM/ML) framework, this part of work examines prismatic <a> loops in hcp α-Zr. All three loop variants are considered, including faulted and perfect, interstitial- and vacancy-type, and first- and second-order prismatic configurations. Nine possible dislocation line segments are characterised in terms of core geometry, solute binding, glide barriers and faulted-to-perfect transition pathways using QM/ML and newly implemented QM/ML-NEB calculations. Shockley and half-Shockley partials, together with basal and prismatic fault ribbons, are found to govern core stabilisation. Fe and H preferentially bind to faulted segments, whereas Sn and Nb favour perfect segments. Solutes can also drive partial motion, recombination and local unfaulting. These results establish a comprehensive picture of <a> loop microstructure, solute trapping and transition mechanisms in α-Zr.

infographic.key_insight: Hybrid QM/ML calculations reveal how partial dislocations and fault ribbons stabilise ⟨a⟩ loop cores in α-Zr, with Fe and H favouring faulted segments and Sn and Nb favouring perfect segments.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These mechanisms can inform models of solute trapping and irradiation-induced microstructure evolution in zirconium nuclear fuel cladding.
method: Hybrid quantum mechanics/machine learning modelling of prismatic ⟨a⟩ loops.
Characterisation of nine dislocation line segments across three loop variants.
QM/ML nudged elastic band calculations of glide barriers and faulted-to-perfect transitions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across nine characterised line segments, calculations identify solute-binding preferences and solute-driven partial motion, recombination and local unfaulting.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract reports atomistic mechanisms but provides no quantitative uncertainty or validation against reactor-scale behaviour.
infographic.paper_title: Comprehensive QM/ML Study of Dislocation Loop Line Segments in α-Zr Part I: <a> Loop Core Geometries, Solute Binding, and Transition Barriers
